posts.author: dcgman
posts.content_md: I propose to get a stepped beamsplitter made up so that various split ratios are available from the same substrate. The more people we can get interested in this beamsplitter, the cheaper the coating run gets. If you're interested, could you fill in the poll in the 'For Sale' section?

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md: Why not continuous? I have one like this and find it really useful - I have it mounted on a microscope stage so I can simply turn a knob to adjust the ratio. If it was reasonable, I'd buy another for a spare.

> Why not continuous? I have one like this and find it really useful - I have it mounted on a microscope stage so I can simply turn a knob to adjust the ratio. If it was reasonable, I'd buy another for a spare.

Those (continuous) variable beamsplitters used to be pretty expensive. I still have one from S&H.

How difficult a task would it be to make a do-it-yourself beamsplitter on DCG? The blue-green region would be easily covered by a DCG hologram. To make things not too complicated, one might start with a single line item.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: The problem from edmund is you need to mount them and fix them. My Edmund cost me about $225 and an hours worth of work to get it on my bench. If we made our own we could have them 3/8" thick and I prefer DE coatings to silvered. I could certainly use more beam splitters. I am limited to three object beams now.

posts.author: dcgman
posts.content_md:
> **Tony:** They're around $75 from Edmund optics....

quoting from the Edmund site: *These are continuously variableneutral density filters. The density (and film thickness) varies linearly across the filter’s length.*

The items you're talking about have metallic coatings, and will absorb a portion of the transmitted beam.

The advantage of all dielectric coatings is that they do not absorb anywhere near as much light as metallic coatings

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Sogokon'A:** Martin wrote:Those (continuous) variable beamsplitters used to be pretty expensive."to be pretty expensive" - this is how much?

For those variable dielectic beamspliters from Spindler & Hoyer (now LINOS - see [http://www.linos-katalog.de/pdf/en-08/c08_e_08.PDF](http://www.linos-katalog.de/pdf/en-08/c08_e_08.PDF)) we must have paid around $600 for a 10x58mm item.

The aluminized beamsplitters used to absorb plenty of light. Moreover, the one manufactured by Edmund back then added lots of cosmetic defects to the beam.

posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md: Sometimes I need a reference beam much less than the 4% minimum most beamsplitters give. Lately I've been using anti-reflection glass to get a reflected reference beam of about 1%. I could take advantage of the p going to zero at 56 degrees but the anti-reflection is simpler.
